# The Heat Is Uneven: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer heat has always been a fact of urban life, but climate change is transforming an annual inconvenience into a public health emergency. Cities are inherently hotter than their surroundings—the urban heat island effect can raise urban temperatures by several degrees Fahrenheit compared to nearby rural areas, and the difference is often largest at night, when human bodies most need relief to recover from daytime heat exposure. Heat already kills more Americans in a typical year than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined, and the toll falls hardest on the elderly, the poor, and residents of neighborhoods that were historically disinvested. The good news is that cities have real tools available: trees, smarter street design, better housing, and expanded public transit can all meaningfully reduce heat stress. The complication is that these tools carry costs, and the tradeoffs they impose—financial, political, and practical—fall unevenly across urban populations. A serious heat policy must therefore be judged not only on how much cooling it produces but on who bears its burdens and who reaps its benefits.
